strengths: Clear and well-motivated technical contribution: decoupling positional guidance (queries) from content representation (key-value pairs) via a 'guided decoding' two-pass decoder cleanly resolves the tension between random-order generation and KV-cache-based parallel decoding that hampers prior work (RAR, RandAR, MaskGIT).

The theoretical motivation (Insights 1-3, including the formal proof that gradients for unmasked-token queries vanish under bidirectional masked modeling) provides principled justification for the architectural design rather than purely empirical tuning.

Strong empirical results: on ImageNet 256x256, ARPG achieves competitive/state-of-the-art FID (1.94) with only 64 steps while offering >20x throughput and >75% memory reduction versus comparably-sized AR baselines (LlamaGen, VAR), and also outperforms RandAR/PAR at similar quality with far fewer steps.

Broad demonstration of versatility: the same framework supports controllable generation (canny/depth conditioning, outperforming ControlVAR/ControlAR), and zero-shot inpainting, outpainting, and resolution expansion without architecture changes, showing the generality of the random-order causal formulation.
Thorough ablation studies (decoder split ratio, shared vs. non-shared KV, number of sampling steps, generation order comparisons) that clarify design choices and quality/efficiency trade-offs.
Reasonable reproducibility support via detailed architecture tables, training hyperparameters, and full pseudo-code for training and parallel decoding in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: Comparisons at 512x512 and for controllable generation only include the L/XL scale of ARPG, and larger scale (XXL) results are not shown across all settings, leaving open questions about scaling behavior at higher capacities/resolutions.

The paper focuses only on class-conditional ImageNet generation and simple conditioning (canny/depth); no text-to-image results are provided (acknowledged as future work), which somewhat limits the demonstrated significance relative to current large-scale generative modeling trends.

Some ablation results (e.g., 'w/o Guided Decoder' degenerating FID >90) are only briefly discussed without deeper analysis of why quality collapses so severely, and the guided-decoder-only variant's advantages/trade-offs could be elaborated further.

The comparison table for random generation order versus fixed orders (Table 7) shows raster order performs comparably or better than random order in some metrics, which raises a question about how much the 'randomized' aspect is actually necessary for raw generation quality versus being primarily useful for zero-shot flexibility; this nuance could be discussed more critically.
Precision/Recall metrics for ARPG-XXL (0.81/0.59) are slightly worse than some VAR variants, and the paper does not deeply analyze diversity-fidelity trade-offs beyond FID/IS reporting.

strengths: Clear theoretical motivation: the paper provides a rigorous derivation (Insight 1-3, gradient analysis) showing why masked-token queries do not receive useful gradients and why explicit positional guidance is necessary for random-order AR modeling, which nicely justifies the proposed 'guided decoding' design.

Elegant architectural contribution: decoupling positional queries (data-independent, target-aware) from content key-values enables causal attention to still support fully random-order training/inference while retaining a KV cache, unlike RandAR (extra instruction tokens) or masked-model approaches (bidirectional attention, no KV cache).

Strong empirical results: on ImageNet 256x256, ARPG achieves competitive/better FID than comparable-size raster-order (LlamaGen) and random-order (RandAR) baselines while using dramatically fewer sampling steps (32-64 vs 88-576), >20x throughput improvement, and >75% memory reduction versus similarly sized AR baselines.

Versatility: the same framework naturally extends to controllable generation (canny/depth conditioning, outperforming ControlVAR/ControlAR), and zero-shot tasks (inpainting, outpainting, class-conditional editing, resolution expansion) without architecture changes, demonstrating broad applicability of the core idea.

Thorough ablations: decoder split ratio, shared KV, number of steps, generation order (raster vs random vs spiral) are all examined, giving good insight into design trade-offs and supporting the main efficiency-quality claims.

Reasonable reproducibility support: pseudocode for training and parallel decoding algorithms is provided in the supplementary material, along with implementation details for zero-shot tasks and controllable generation.
weaknesses: The 512x512 comparison (Table 3) is somewhat thin, using fine-tuning from the 256 model rather than comparable from-scratch training for all baselines, making some conclusions about efficiency-quality tradeoffs at higher resolution less rigorous.

The main results table lacks some very recent strong baselines in continuous-token or bit-token AR generation (e.g., MAGVIT-style or diffusion-in-AR hybrids), and text-to-image scaling is explicitly left for future work, somewhat limiting the demonstrated significance beyond ImageNet class-conditional generation.

The zero-shot generalization experiments (inpainting/outpainting/editing) are shown qualitatively (Fig. 5, supplementary figures) without quantitative metrics (e.g., no FID/LPIPS for inpainting quality), making it hard to judge how competitive ARPG is against dedicated inpainting/outpainting methods.

Ablation on generation order (Table 7) shows raster order is comparable to or better than random order, which somewhat undercuts the core motivating claim that random order is beneficial for generation quality itself (its main benefit seems to be parallelism/zero-shot flexibility rather than quality).

strengths: Well-motivated decoupled two-pass decoding design that cleanly separates content representation from position-guided prediction, avoiding the sequence-length doubling of RandAR while retaining random-order generation and KV-cache compatibility.

Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art FID (1.83 at 256x256) with substantial speedups (~30x) and memory reduction (75%) over comparable AR baselines like LlamaGen and VAR, across multiple model scales (L/XL/XXL).

Broad demonstration of versatility: class-conditional generation, text-to-image generation with limited data (4M samples), controllable generation (Canny/depth), and zero-shot inpainting/outpainting/resolution expansion, showing the method generalizes beyond the primary training task.

Solid ablation studies (architecture depth split, shared KV, positional encoding, decoding steps, attention pattern generalization, sampling order) that support design choices with reasonably clear insight into the tradeoffs.
Includes a theoretical proof (Appendix C) motivating the training-inefficiency claim of masked modeling, and provides attention map analyses (Fig. 3, Fig. 11) supporting the core design insight.
Reasonably good reproducibility support: detailed architecture/hyperparameter tables, pseudo-code for training and generation provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Some efficiency/throughput comparisons (e.g., Table 2, Table 3) do not always control fully for parameter count or training data differences (e.g., text-to-image comparison uses only 7% of LlamaGen's data), which could make comparisons to baselines less apples-to-apples, though this is partially acknowledged.

The zero-shot generalization claims (inpainting/outpainting/resolution expansion) are shown mostly via qualitative examples (Fig. 8, Fig. 13) without corresponding quantitative metrics (e.g., FID for inpainting/outpainting) to substantiate quality beyond visual inspection.

The paper builds heavily on existing ideas (RandAR's random order training, MaskGIT-style parallel decoding, XLNet-style query/content stream decoupling); while the decoupled two-pass mechanism is a genuine contribution, the overall novelty is incremental relative to this line of work.

Limited discussion of failure cases or limitations of the proposed method (e.g., when random-order or parallel decoding degrades quality, or scaling limits), reducing the completeness of the evaluation.

The scalability analysis (Fig. 10) is based only on training loss curves rather than downstream quality metrics at larger scale, making the claim about potential for further improvement mostly speculative.

Controllable generation baseline comparisons (Table 4) use different parameter counts and training setups across methods (VAR, ControlAR, ControlARPG), complicating fair attribution of gains to the proposed method itself versus base model quality.

strengths: The decoupled two-pass decoder design (content representation pass + position-guided cross-attention pass) is a clean and well-motivated architectural innovation that cleanly separates content encoding from position-conditioned prediction, avoiding the sequence-doubling overhead of RandAR while retaining fully random-order training/inference with causal attention (no bidirectional attention needed for KV caching).

Strong empirical results: ARPG-XXL achieves FID 1.83 with only 32 steps on ImageNet 256x256, outperforming LlamaGen, VAR, and other parallel-decoding AR baselines (PAR, NAR, RandAR) in both quality and efficiency (30x speedup, 75% memory reduction), across three model scales, which is a fairly comprehensive comparison.

The paper provides good analytical grounding for its design choices: the attention-score analysis of RandAR (Fig. 3) motivating that mask tokens are redundant to attend to, and a theoretical proof (Appendix C) showing zero gradients flow to unmasked-token queries in standard masked modeling, both support the core insight driving the architecture.

Broad demonstration of generalization: the same model supports zero-shot inpainting/outpainting/resolution expansion, controllable generation (canny/depth-conditioned), and text-to-image generation with limited additional training, showing the framework's versatility beyond simple class-conditional benchmarks.

Extensive ablations (decoding steps, attention pattern generalization from causal to block-wise, architecture depth split between passes, shared KV projection, RoPE vs cosine PE, sampling order) that support the design decisions and offer insight into what components matter.
Reasonably good reproducibility support: detailed architecture/hyperparameter tables in the appendix and PyTorch-style pseudocode for training and generation.
weaknesses: The text-to-image comparison (Table 3) is somewhat weak: ARPG-XL uses only 4M training samples vs. 60M for LlamaGen-XL and 2B for SD-v1.5, and while this is framed as an efficiency win, the 'Overall' GenEval score (0.31) is actually lower than both LlamaGen (0.32) and SD-v1.5 (0.43), so the T2I claims of competitiveness are somewhat overstated relative to the actual numbers shown.

Some ambiguity remains regarding the theoretical claim in Appendix C: the proof shows the final-layer gradient for masked-token queries is zero in a single generic transformer layer, but the paper's own follow-up sentence notes that shallow-layer queries for unmasked tokens still receive indirect gradients, which somewhat undercuts the strength of 'Insight 2' as a fully rigorous general critique of masked modeling training efficiency (it applies most cleanly to the last layer only).

The paper claims robustness/superiority of generalizing from causal (training) to block-wise (inference) attention, but the underlying justification is empirical/intuitive ('local bidirectional context is beneficial') rather than theoretically grounded, and it is unclear how consistently this generalization gap behaves across different data domains or resolutions beyond ImageNet.

Qualitative comparisons for zero-shot inpainting/outpainting/editing/resolution-expansion lack quantitative metrics (e.g., no FID/LPIPS for edited/outpainted regions) in the main text, making it hard to objectively judge how these zero-shot capabilities compare to dedicated inpainting/outpainting baselines beyond visual inspection.

Limited discussion of failure cases or limitations of the proposed method (e.g., when random-order training underperforms, sensitivity to the ordering distribution, or scaling behavior beyond 1.3B parameters) -- the conclusion section is very brief and does not discuss weaknesses.

The controllable generation and 512x512 comparisons involve fine-tuning strategies (e.g., 50-epoch fine-tuning from 256 pretrained models) that may not be perfectly matched with the baselines' training setups, which could confound the fairness of some throughput/quality comparisons in Table 2 (512x512) and Table 4.
